Discounting of Indian Cotton in International Market 
*241. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of TEXTILES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian cotton is discounted in international 
market due to poor quality of ginning, imperfect packing, contamination and 
higher trash contents thus unable to withstand international competition; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the remedial measures taken or proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI KASHIRAM RANA): (a) to (c) 
A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Government of India have launched the Technologv Mission 
on Cotton (TMC) in the country to address the % issues of quality and 
productivity of cotton; the Mini Mission—III for improvement of market  
infrastructure  and  Mini 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [8 August, 2001] 
Mission—IV  for  modernisation   of  Cotton   Ginning  and  Pressing factories, 
are being implemented by the Ministry of Textiles. 
The improved market infrastructure would provide better facilities for 
handling and storage of cotton so that contamination and trash contents are 
minimized. Similarly, modern cotton Ginning & Pressing factories would 
provide better ginning and pressing facilities so that quality of cotton is not 
affected during processing and pre ssing. These measures are aimed at 
increasing the competitiveness of Indian cotton in the international market.

SHRI KASHIRAM RANA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the hon. Member wants to 
know why adequate export of cotton is not being made. So far as the quality 
of our cotton is concerned, it is not as superior as the Australian and Egyptian 
cotton. Moreover, Sir, our cotton is contaminated and inadequate market 
infrastructure facilities prevail in the domestic market. The Government has 
launched a Technology Mission on Cotton in order to control all these 
deficiencies and to improve the quality of our cotton, to remove the 
contamination from the cotton and to provide the best possible infrastructural 
facilities to growers and to exporters to boost cotton exports. One more 
reason for our difficulty is that the price of our cotton is higher than what is 
prevalent in the international market. It  is because per hectare yield of our 
cotton is very low. The average per h ectare yield of our cotton is about 300 
kilograms, while that of the Australian cotton is about 1700 kilograms and 
that of the Egyptian cotton is about 1800 kilograms. While the international 
average yield of cotton is nearly 560 kilograms per hectare, the national 
average yield of our cotton is 300 kilograms. The yield of cotton varies from 
State to State. For example, in Andhra Pradesh it is more than 400 kilograms. 
That means there is a scope to increas e the per hectare yield of the Indian 
cotton. The Government of India is eager  to increase the per hectare yield of 
our cotton. Under the Technology Mission on Cotton, the Government of 
India is trying to improve the quality of cotton. We also want to see that its 
cost of production is reduced. We started with this Technology Mission 12 or 
13 months back and are very confident that within a short period of time our 
growers will be able to export their cotton at a very reasonable price.

Centre-State relations 
*244. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the resolution 
adopted unanimously at the 'Mahanadu' the Telegu Desam party conclave held at 
Vishakhapatnam in May, 2001 urging the Central Government to redefine Centre-
State relationship through a greater devolution of power to the State 
Governments including higher allocation of financial resources; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) whether it is proposed to implement the same and if not, the reasons 
therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) The Central Government has not received any 
reference regarding resolutions adopted at the "Mahanadu", the TDP conclave held 
at Vishakapatnam in May, 2001. 
However, the Government of India had set up the Sarkaria Commission to 
go into the issue of Centre-State relations. The Sarkaria Commission's 
recommendations aim at developing harmonious Centre-State relations and are 
being considered by the Inter-State Council, which have all Chief Ministers of States 
and Administrators of the Union Territories as members. Out of 247 
recommendations made by the Commission, the Inter-State Council has so far 
taken a view on 171 recommendations. 95 of these recommendations have been 
implemented, 16 recommendations have been rejected and 60 recommendations are 
under implementation by States and Central Ministries. 
The recommendations of the Sarkaria Commission considered and decided by 
the Inter-State Council which deal with devolution of more administrative and 
financial powers to States relate administrative Relations, Reservations of Bills,

Tenth Finance Commission, States used to get a specified share of Union

(i) Gavaranjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY):
The erstwhile Self-employment Programmes of the Integrated Rural
Development Programme (IRDP), the Training of Rural Youth for Self 
Employment (TRYSEM), the Development of Women and Children in Rural 
Areas (DWCRA), the Supply of Improved Tool-kits to Rural Artisans (SITRA), 
the Ganga Kalyan Yojana (GKY) and the Million Wells Scheme (MWS) were 
restructured from April, 1999 to form a new Programme known as the 
Swaranjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY). 
In rural areas, the SGSY is a Cred it-cum-Subsidy Programme. Credit is a 
critical component in the SGSY and Subsidy is a minor and enabling element. 
Accordingly, the SGSY envisages greater involvement of the Banks right from the 
planning and preparation of projects to posts—credit monitoring including loan 
recovery. The objective of the SGSY is to bring the assisted poor above the Poverty

of Bank Credit and Government Subsidy. The loan component for Swarozgaris 
under the Scheme are provided by the Financial Institutions. Subsidy under the 
SGSY is uniform at 30% of the project cost, subject to a maximum of Rs. 7,50(y-.

maximum of Rs. 10,000'-. For groups of swarojgaris (SHGs), the subsidy is 
50% of the project cost, subject to a ceiling of Rs. 1.25 lakhs. There is no 
monetary limit on subsidy for irrigation projects. The SGSY focus on the 
vulnerable groups among the rural poor. Accordingly, the SOSTs will account 
for at least 50% of the Swarozgaris, women 40% and the disabled 3%.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): 
(a) to (c) The Traffic Management Plan formulated by the Delhi Traffic 
Police focuses on three major areas viz., (i) effective enforcement of rules 
and regulations; (ii) introduction of modern road engineering and traffic 
regulation techniques; and (iii) inculcating road safety awareness amongst the 
road users through education: 
(i) Enforcement: The enforcement drives undertaken by the Delhi Police 
are particularly directed at red lig ht jumping, over-speeding, reckless 
driving, driving by minors, use of defective number plates, driving 
without helmet, use of mobile phones while driving, disciplining 
buses and commercial vehicles, etc. In addition, cameras to detect 
traffic violators and speeding vehicles, interceptors and close circuit 
TV cameras for traffic monitoring have been installed at selected 
locations. 
(ii) Engineering & Regulation: With a view to ensuring a free flow and 
unrestricted movement of traffic as also to minimize congestion, 
accidents and pollution, the following measures have been taken:— 
• introduction of one-way traffic at congested roads; 
• Closure of around 150 gaps on central verges of busy roads; 
• re-routing of buses at congested office complexes; 
40 

[8 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
• imposition of restrictions on plying of heavy, medium and light goods 
vehicles during specific hours; 
• restrictions on slow moving vehicles in selected areas; 
• regulation   of   parking   space   to   reduce   congestion   of 
carriageway space; 
• banning of right turns and 'U' turns on important signalized junctions; 
• erection of road signs for the guidance of general public; 
• provision of central verges, iron railings, bus lanes, Zebra crossings; 
• installation of traffic signals, blinkers and pelican signals at accident-
prone locations; 
• synchronization   of  traffic  signals  on   19  important   traffic corridors; 
• installation of computerized Area Traffic Control System on an 
experimental basis; etc. 
In addition, the Delhi Police regularly takes up with the Government of 
NCT of Delhi the matter of construction of flyovers, subways and grade 
separators for providing smooth flow of traffic in the national capital. 
(iii) Education: Delhi Police undertakes spread of road safety education 
through road safety literature; traffic training parks specially to educate 
school children; advertisements; traffic information dissemination; 
appointment of traffic wardens, st udent volunteers, traffic advisory 
committees; encouraging public to lodge their complaints through 
complaint cards, etc. It also organizes regular training programmes for 
professional drivers, drivers in government employment and other 
motorists. It has also identified 10 most accident-prone spots which are 
being analysed continuously to devise measures to reduce fatalities at 
these locations.

SYED SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Pricing of coking coal and A, B & C grades of non-coking coal was 
deregulated w.e.f. 22.3.1996. Subsequently the pricing of hard-coke, soft coke and 
'D' grade of non-coking coal was deregulated in February, 1997. Pricing of coal has

IPP's demand to restore tax relaxations on gross income 
1908. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that IPP's are now demanding that Government 
restore the tax relaxation on gross income as originally provided under 10 
(23G) which was hit by the CBDT notifications restricting benefits of tax 
reduction on the net income only; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [8 August, 2001] 
(b) the IPP's in States like Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu are 
already in default by the SEB's creating apprehension and financial losses in their 
project; and 
(c) if so, Government reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) Several Independent Power Producers 
have made representations to the Union Ministry of Finance with respect to 
tax exemption under Section 10 (23G) in reference to the newly introduced 
Section 14A in the Income Tax Act, 1961. This amendment was made specifically 
to provide that no deduction shall be allowed in respect of expenditure incurred in 
relation to exempt income. The exemption under Section 10 (23G) was always 
allowable on net basis only. This was specifically clarified through Circular No. 
780 dated October 4, 1999 issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes to 
provide that only the net income after taking into account all expenses 
incurred to earn the said income would be exempt under Section 10(23G) of the 
Income Tax Act. Only the net income i.e. gross income minus the 
expenditure, is taxed and on the same analogy, the exemption is also in respect 
of the net income. As some of the assessees were not accepting the circular 
issued in October, 1999 this was leading to a lot of litigation. To avoid such 
litigations, Section 14A was inserted through Finance Act, 2001 with 
retrospective effect from April 1, 1962 to reiterate the above mentioned 
principles of taxation which was also specifically stated through circular No. 780 
dated October 4, 1999.

Revamping of Poverty Alleviation Programmes 
1921. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN:  
          SHRI N.R. DASARI:  
          SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to revamp poverty alleviation programmes in 
view of the fact that large chunks of funds go down annually to the drain without 
reaching those below the poverty line; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what is Government's reaction to the Comptroller and Auditor General's 
report pointing out Centre's apathy either to take up responsibility or transfer 
these schemes totally to the States? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVE LOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) and (b) The major poverty alleviation Programmes like the 
Swamjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), the Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana 
(JGSY) and the Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS) have been launched from 
April, 1999 after revamping their erstwhile corresponding Programmes. The 
SGSY, has been launched in place of  the erstwhile Integrated Rural 
Development Programme (IRDP), Training of Rural Youth for Self Employment 
(TRYSEM), Development of Women & Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), 
Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITRA) & Ganga Kalyan 
Yojana (GKY), besides the Million Wells Scheme (MWS). The major shift of the 
SGSY from the earlier Programmes is in respect of its emphasis on integrated 
approach and social mobilization of the rural poor through Self Help Group (SHG). 
The JGSY has been launched in place of the erstwhile Jawahar Rozgar Yojana 
(JRY) and is implemented now exclusively by the Gram Panchayats for 
infrastructure development at the village level. Similarly, the EAS has been now 
made allocation based from demand driven. The new programmes have also 
been designed, keeping in view, the po sitive aspects and the deficiency of 
erstwhile corresponding programmes. 
150 

[8 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The revamped Programmes are a little over two years old and at this stage it 
would be too early to consider any revamping of these Programmes. 
(c) The implementation of the Programmes is a joint responsibility of the 
Centre and the States. While, the programmes are formulated by the Centre, the 
States are responsible for their implementation. At the stage of formulation of the 
programmes, the States are extensively consulted, besides experts in the field. 
Both are equally accountable for the poverty alleviation agenda of the country. 
The States also share the responsibility of the funds for all the Programmes 
i.e. in the ratio of 75% by the Centre and 25% by the States. The Centre and the 
States, therefore, are equally concerned about the quality of implementation of 
these Programmes. In view of the above and because of the federal set up of the 
country, the dual control over the Programmes is unavoidable.

Remedial Measures Taken by Government With Regard Thereto 
Ǜी सुरेश पचौरी (मध्य Ģदेश): आदरणीय सभापित महोदय, मȅ देश मȂ आयुध िडपुओं 
मȂ आग लगने की हाल की घटनाओं और सरकार ǎारा तत्संबंधी िकए गए उपचारी उपायȗ 
पर रक्षा मंतर्ी का ध्यान आकिर्षत करता हूं। 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS AND MINISTER OF 
DEFENCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, hon. Members 
would recall that yesterday I had informed them about a minor ammunition 
related accident, in the Laboratory locat ed in Ammunition Technical Area of 
Central Ordnance Depot, Jabalpur that had occurred on 6 th August, 2001. In 
response to that statement, hon. Members had suggested, and I had concurred 
that a fuller discussion about fires in Ordnance depots, during the last two 
years, specifically from 28 th April, 2000, should take place. No doubt, hon. 
Members have taken note that during the current session of the Parliament, I 
have already answered a number of questions, on this very issue, in both the 
Houses. 
As hon. Members are aware there were seven incidents of fire, of 
different intensity, in Ordnance Depots , during this period of two years. 
Details about these fire accidents I will sh ortly detail. I might add at the very 
outset that except in the case of the fire at Ammunition Depot, Bharatpur 
there has been no loss to civilian life or property in any of these accidents: 
(a) Ammunition Depot, Bharatpur (28,h April, 2000): Two civilians died 
and seven civilians were injured. The loss to civilian property was 
estimated at Rs. 70 lakhs. 
(b) Ammunition Depot, Dehu Road (3rd May, 2000) 
(c) Central Ordnance Depot, Kanpur. (28th May, 2000) 
198 

[8 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) 2 Ammunition Sub Depot (18 Field Ammunition Depot), Mamoon 
(Pathankot (29m April, 2001). 
(e) 2 Ammunition Sub Depot (24 Field Ammunition Depot) Birdhwal, 
(Ganganagar) (24th May, 2001). 
(f) Ordnance Depot Shakurbasti, Delhi (3rd June, 2001) 
(g) Central Ordnance Depot, Jabalpur (6m August, 2001) 
Courts of Inquiry had been ordered for in all these fire incidents. 
Courts of Inquiry have been comple ted in all cases, except that of 2 
Ammunition Sub Depot, (24 Field Ammunition Depot), Birdhwal 
(Ganganagar), Ordnance Depot, Shakurbasti, Delhi and Central Ordnance 
Depot, Jabalpur. 
I would like to share with the hon. Members major findings of these 
Courts of Inquiry, also the action taken on them. 
Ammunition Depot, Bharatpur (28th April.2000) : The likely cause was 
due to short circuit/sparking on pole No.4 near Guard post No.11. It has, 
however, not been possible to confirm th is through specific, direct evidence. 
The Court of Inquiry has, inter alia, made the following recommendations:- 
(1) Manpower and Equipment deficiency be made up. 
(2) Strict control be maintained over cooking and heating at the 
Guard Posts. 
(3) Communications capability needs to be strengthened. 
(4) Employment of Casual Labour for clearance of undergrowth be 
permitted. 
(5) Construction of additional ammunition sheds be taken up. 
Deficiencies in manpower and equipment have been made up 
partially. Construction of 21 Explosive Store Houses for storage of 
ammunition is in progress. Works on perimeter fencing and for enhancement 
of electric and water supply have been sanctioned. Additional communication 
equipment has also been provided. Ad ministrative action against the Army 
personnel has been completed. 
199 

RAJYA SABHA [8 August, 2001) 
Ammunition Depot, Dehu Road (3rd May, 2000). This was an incident of 
grass fire caused by high temperatures and spread by strong winds. No one 
was held responsible for the fire. The Court of Inquiry has, inter alia, made the 
following recommendations: - 
(1) Fire lanes be constructed in this Ammunition Depot. 
(2) There shall be a ban on controlled fires. 
(3) Deficiencies of fire fighting equipments be made up. 
(4) Provision for casual labour/grass cutting machines be made. The 
first two recommendations have been fully implemented.  On 
the remaining too, satisfactory progress has been made. 
Central Ordnance Depot, Kanpur (28th May, 2000). The cause of the fire 
cannot be specified as the Court of I nquiry did not identify the exact cause. 
The possibility of sabotage/arson has, however, not been ruled out. The Court 
of Inquiry made the following recommendations: - 
(1) To expedite modernization of the depot. 
(2) Equipment deficiency be made up. 
(3) Better liaison with civil fire services be maintained. 
(4) Grass cutting equipment be procured. 
(5) Timely auction of salavage items be conducted. 
A project for modernization of Central Ordnance Depot, Kanpur, has 
been approved by the Government at an expenditure of Rs. 187 crores. Work 
has started on the project and is likely to be completed by December, 2003. 
The project envisages complete mech anization of the stores handling, 
construction of additional and tiered storage accommodation, improvements 
in security environment by better lighting, reduced deployment of security 
personnel, higher perimeter walls etc.  Action against the defaulting personnel 
has been initiated. 
2 Ammunition Sub Depot (18 FAD). Mamoon (Pathankot) (29 th 
April, 2001). The Court of Inquiry has made the following main 
recommendations: - 
(1) Deficiencies in fire fighting equipment be made up. 
(2) Shortage of security staff be made up. 
(3) Plant and Machinery for clearance of grass be procured. 
(4) Holding of unit ammunition in depots to be avoided. 
(5) Storage and handling of ammunition to be as per regulations. 
(6) Ammunition Regulations need updating. 
(7) Gazette   notification   under   Indian   Works   of   Defence Act, 
1903, to be issued. 
200 

[8 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The Court of Inquiry has held th ree Officers, one JCO and three 
ORs responsible. The Court of Inquiry has been finalized only recently. 
However, departmental directions on security, fire fighting and management 
of ammunition have been reiterated. 
2 Ammunition Sub Depot (24 Fiel d Ammunition Depot), Birdhwal 
(Ganganagar) (24 m May, 2001). The cause of fire will only be ascertained 
after completion of the Court of Inquiry, which is under progress. 
Ordnance Depot, Shakurbasti, Delhi (3 rd June, 2001). Similarly, the 
cause of fire will only be ascertained after completion of the Court of Inquiry, 
which is also under progress. 
Central Ordnance Depot, Jabalpur (6th August, 2001). Court of Inquiry 
has been ordered. 
The following additional steps have also been taken to prevent such 
incidents in Ordnance Depots: - 
All  depots  have  been  directed  to  update  safety  and  security 
instructions. 
All depots have been inspected by a Board of Officers to check 
adequacy of safety and security arrangements. 
Shortages in fire fighting equipment are being made up and 
defective equipment repaired. 
Unserviceable ammunition is being disposed of on priority. 
Allotment of additional funds for creation of more storage 
accommodation for shifting ammunition,  presently stored on open 
plinths, under canvas, to proper Explosive Stores Houses. 
I wish to share with the hon. Me mbers certain basic shortcomings 
that the development of ammunition depots have had. To take stock, in the 
ten years period, from 1989 to 1999, an average of Rs.8 to 9 crores only, per 
year, were spent for ammunition storage related projects. Mindful of the 
seriousness of the problem, and with a view to rectifying this shortfall in 
modernisation and provision of ammunition storage accommodation, the 
Government, in the last two years, have already allocated an amount of about 
Rs.350 crores. It is planned that by the end of 2004, all ammunition would be    
shifted    into covered accommodation. 
201 

RAJYA SABHA (8 August, 2001] 
I would like to assure the hon. Members that the Government is 
seized of this problem which, unfortunately, was not attended to for almost 
five decades. There is an urgent need to change not only the means of storage 
but also the method of it. And, we are committed to doing precisely that.  
Thank you, Sir.

SHRI JIBON ROY (West Bengal): Thank you, Mr. Vice-Chairman. 
I am not surprised by the regular incidents of fire in the ammunition depots, 
but I am shocked because of two reas ons. Firstly, it is an open secret, 
everybody knows about the cause of the fire, except the Members of 
Parliament. Everybody knows about it. Still the Ministry and the concerned 
Department kept sleeping for years together, without trying to improve the 
situation. The second reason for the shock is that the incidents are taking 
place one after the other. At Bharatpu r itself, according to the previous 
Defence Minister's statement, the loss amounted to Rs. 370 crores, though the 
private estimates put the loss at Rs. 2,000 crores. Sir, no official statement has 
come out from the Government as to what actually caused fires. Absence of a 
comprehensive statement raises many questions about the storage 
management. Therefore, I said that I was shocked for two reasons. Firstly, no 
step was taken to ensure that such incidents do not recur and secondly no 
statement was made by the Minister concerned as to 
214 

[8 August. 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
w h a t  c a u s e d  t h e  f i r e s .     O n l y  t o d ay, as a result of the Calling Attention 
Motion, the statement has been made by the hon. Minister. 
Sir, the general perception is that the fire has taken place because no 
proper storage arrangement is there for the arms and ammunitions. I do agree 
that there is no proper storage arrangement. Moreover, adequate funds are not 
provided for the purpose. The storage management is not modernised. 
Moreover, there is an absence of skilled manpower. This is another problem. 
Hon. Defence Minister is aware that pe rhaps the biggest fire in history had 
taken place three years ago at Jabalpur. At that time it was found that there 
was no proper storage management and that there was no skilled labour for 
the purpose. Storage of ammunitions requires specialised stacking by 
specialised people. But, that manpower is not there in most of the depots. 
Ammunitions are simply unloaded and kept outside in the grass unguarded. 
Sir, you find that the incidents of these fires have taken place only during 
summer and not during winter. This s hows there was an unscientific and 
wrong stacking of ammunitions stored. As you know, during the summer 
season, there is a possibility of fi res taking place, no proper safety 
management systems were kept at pl ace. All these things could not even 
attract the attention of the Ministry. I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether henceforth an independent safety management system will 
be established. If you can have an independent audit system, why can't you 
have an independent safety management system? I am told even the vacancies 
of the people responsible to run the fire engines have not been filled up. You 
have to take care of that aspect also. 
Finally, a lot of suspicion has come about in the minds of the people. 
Some say it is because of the faulty safety arrangements; some say it is 
because of lack of proper storage arrangements. Moreover, there is a 
possibility of sabotage, which may take place from two direc tions. One is by 
the agents of the companies who supply arms and ammunition from abroad. I 
am glad that except the ammuniti on at Bharatpur, probably all the 
ammunitions are produced in our country. Only missiles were imported. In 
India, most of the ammunitions are produced by our public sector companies 
and not by private companies. But, the moment you open up the ammunition 
production area to private and foreign companies, that area would get exposed 
to new forces. Nobdoy knows the actual cause of the fires. The Statement of 
the hon. Minister of Defence on the Bharatpur incident also could not point 
out the cause of the fire. Nobody could detect

and manufacturing of weapons to everybody, then, you will have many 
agencies which would work for this purpose. I would like the Defence 
Minister to take note of it and ponder over the matter. Finally, may I know 
from the Defence Minister whether the Government would take measures to 
bring safety to our ammunition system and storage system? Thank you very

SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, thank you very much. I am sorry to say that the statement 
made by the hon. Defence Minister is not at all satisfactory. Many doubts 
arise following such a statement on a very, very serious and sensitive matter. 
While speaking on this Calling Attention motion, I am haunted by the 
direction of the hon. Chairman, "One Member should not take more than five 
minutes." The time constraint is there. I am afraid, it may not be possible for 
me to seek clarifications, within fi ve minutes, from the Defence Minister. 
Therefore, I would request the indulgence of the Chair. 
Sir, I do not know why the hon. Members of this House are telling 
that within a span of two years seven accidents have taken place. In fact, right 
from April, 2000 to 6 ,h August, 2001, seven accident s have taken place. It is 
only one year and three months. Within this short time, seven accidents have 
taken place. I am not a person to buy the concept of accidents. 
I remember an English axiom that once you are fooled, the blame is 
not yours. You cannot be blamed for that. But if you are fooled twice, the 
same way, you will be blamed. Here we find seven accidents have taken 
place. The Defence Department which is believed to be the most competent 
Department of this country has been fooled. Not only that, over and above 
this, these inquiries into the accidents have been conducted by themselves. It 
is only the part of the administration who are responsible for this sort of 
unsafe keeping of the ammunition. They have conducted inquiries. The 
inquiry, perhaps, suppressed more than it revealed.

Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, overall, there was a deficiency of 238 fire-
fighting trucks in the year 1998-99. Thereafter, an order for 50 such trucks 
was placed in 1999, and 88 fire-fighting trucks were contracted for in 2000. 
In 2000-2001, there was a deficiency of 137 trucks, and they have also been 
contracted for. Earlier, a ban had been imposed by the Government of India 
on further recruitment. This is one of the curious factors of the functioning of 
Governments all over the world, that when blanket orders are issued, they 
apply across the-board. Thereafter, whether a position is needed or not 
r.aeded; it ought to be blanketly banned or not banned, each case, thereafter, 
becomes a case by itself and then we ha ve to grow. So, there was a ban on 
recruitment; hence, there was a deficiency  of fire-fighting staff. I accept that, 
but we have inherited that deficiency. We went back to the Ministry of 
Finance. This blanket ban was got relaxed. Some vacancies were also created, 
and we are filling up the same. But you will appreciate that -I do not want to 
go into any further details about the

deficiency of fire-fighting staff, but I do wish to take a minute or two to 
explain how the overall deficiencies or  shortcomings, as pointed out by my 
gallant friend, General Roy Chowdhury, and a number of other hon. 
Members, came about. -- I am not enga ging myself in fault-finding. I am 
simply pointing out a reality and I am attempting to explain as to what was 
the rationale behind the allocation of funds earlier. Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
the Indian Armed Forces, very broadly, have seen three major expansions 
and, thereafter, a growth pattern has be en set up which is not consistent. The 
first expansion took place in post-1962; the second - post-65 and the third - 
post- 71. In the mid 80's, a considerable effort was made, under the leadership 
of late Shri Rajiv Gandhiji, when he was the Prime Minister- I think, in the 
year 1985-86, - I might be slightly in  error about the exac t year --and there 
was a quantum leap in the budgetary allocation for the Ministry of Defence. 
Then, there was also a re-adjustment, and subsequent Governments had to cut 
back on defence allocation. This is not a value-judgment. Subsequent 
Governments had to cut back because of the compulsions, which were 
overriding. We were all witness to what was happening then. This having 
been said, let us also accept that de spite these expansions of the Armed 
Forces,-- 1962, 1965, 1971, - roughly, around 1985 -- it was not that as if the 
allotment to the Armed Forces was infinite or unlimited or that the Armed 
Forces could have whatever they want  to. So, whenever these allocations 
were made to the Armed Forces, necessar ily, within the Ministry of Defence, 
priorities were fixed as to on what that money ought to be spen*. Should we 
spend it on capital expenditure; should we spend it on housing; should we 
spend it on acquisition of new aircraft , new tanks or should we spend it on 
ammunition storage? Hon. Members would understand that the allocation of

not again find any fault. It has been receiving a second place because money

anybody. I understand why it had happened in this fashion. There is another 
broad aspect.   This, when happened, was indeed a lapse. I have

Let me share one fact with the hon.  M e m b e r s .  I t  i s  n o t  a s  i f  a l l  
ammunition depots are of World War II or World War I vintage. But, field 
depots, as my friend, Gen. Roy Chowdhury knows, necessarily, have to be

troops, should the troops have to perform their tasks during operations. So, it is 
not possible for the ammunitions to be moved during the operation from the

serves a purpose. So, some of the advance depots, as it were, I ( am deliberately

there is no covered space, because they have come up subsequently. But some 
of the older depots are located near habitations or habitation centres or are in 
cities. It is in that context that I must quote the Act of 1903. The Act is of a 
much older vintage than the year denotes.  This Act requires that if there be a 
military installation, that must be notified and that within a specified distance 
of that military installation, no civilian population, habitation, construction, 
building, etc. should come up. The reality, as of today, is that, it has 
encroached on this existing inheritence. In some of the older depots, 
particularly in Punjab, UP, even in Rajasthan, which did not have any of the 
older depots, in Madhya Pradesh, and also, possibly, in West Bengal, the 
prohibition or preventing other population from creeping up to the depots was 
not observed. It was not observed, because the Administration of those areas is 
the responsibility of the States of the Union. The States of the Union had, 
despite repeated requests by the Ministry of Defence to please prevent this from 
happening, permitted this to happen. I am not charging them, but the State 
Governments simply did not act. There is a requirement that around the 
military airfields, there should be no construction up to a distance of 500 
metres. I can cite you military airfields all over the country, where not only has 
this been breached in totality, but construction and civil population and 
habitation has been permitted to come up to Air Force Station perimeters.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI): Now, we 
will take up further consideration of the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Bill,

 SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, thank you. Yesterday, I could not complete my speech because 
the House had to take up some other issue. I will quickly recapitulate what has 
been discussed yesterday. I am s upporting the Bill because the objects 
underlying the Bill and the amendments are laudable. It stipulates the time-
limit of 60 days for disposing of an application for alimony or maintenance 
and education of minor children. 
Sir, the intention of the Bill is good. The objectives are good. But 
the question I am having is whether by mere enactment, it is possible to 
achieve the objects. Sir, why I am sayi ng this is that there are already such 
provisions existing in the Hindu Marriage Act. Section 21(b) of this Act 
stipulates time-limit. Section 21 (b) (2) says, "Every petition under this Act 
shall be tried as expeditiously as possible and an endeavour shall be made to 
conclude the trial within six months from the date of service of notice of 
232 

[8 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
the petition on the respondent." Section 21 (b) (3) deals with an appeal. I 
quote : "Every appeal under this Act shall be heard as expeditiously as 
possible. An endeavour shall be made to conclude the hearing within three 
months from the date of service of the notice of appeal on the respondent." 
Sir, there is no ambiguity about this. It clearly stipulates the time-limit. 
Inspite of this, in reality, we know wh at is happening. Sir, appeals in High 
Courts take not less than lo to 12 years before they are disposed of. This is the 
stark reality. What I feel is that there is a need to provide more teeth to the 
present Bill. 
Sir, my suggestion, in this regard, is two-fold. One is that there must 
be a provision to the effect that if the application filed for alimony or 
maintenance and education of minor children is not disposed of within the 
stipulated time of 60 days, 50 per cent of the amount claimed by the wife 
should be paid to her. Further, if the husband defaults, then, the amount 
should be recovered from him as if the amount is due under the Revenue 
Recovery Act. Sir, the court should have the power to order his imprisonment 
or fine or both in case he violates this provision. Sir, unless the laws are made 
stringent, the object of this Bill cannot be achieved. 
With regard to appeals, I suggest that before anybody approaches for 
appeal, before an appeal is entertained, 50 per cent of the amount should be 
paid to the wife. Similar provision is there in the Industrial Disputes Act. 
Another important issue which I am raising is about the matrimonial 
disputes. Unfortunately, the matrimonial  disputes in the country are on the 
increase. I am of the opini on that this kind of disputes can be resolved more 
by conciliation and counselling than by adjudication. Therefore, the 
Government should take necessary steps to set up bodies or agencies for this 
purpose at the sub-court level. It should be made mandatory for the parties to 
go in for conciliation and counselling before adjudication of the case. 
A similar provision is there in the Industrial Disputes Act and I am 
sure this will reduce the number of litigations and this will also reduce the 
burden on the court. 
Sir, I would like to add one or two points and conclude. There are 
certain bottlenecks which I would like to bring to the notice of the hon. Law 
Minister. Under sections 17 and 20 of  the Indian Divorce Act, the decree 
granted for divorce or nullity of marriage is subject to confirmation by a

provision. This will only result in pr otracting the litigation. This is doing 
more harm than good. Therefore, such provisions should go, should be 
amended. 
The last point I am making is th at some accountability should be 
fixed on the courts for disposing of so serious and sensitive matters as 
matrimonial disputes. There must be a system of submitting a list of the 
pending matrimonial matters to the concerned portfolio Judges of the High

Sir, if these steps are taken, I am sure, the time limit stipulated under

While concluding with these words, I support the Bill.

DISCUSSION ON THE STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER 
Recent Summit-Level Talks Held Between India And Pakistan in Agra 
THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN 
SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, diplomacy today is a serious discipline in most 
universities in the world, and a case-st udy method of examining the various 
issues has also gained prominence all over the world. I submit to you. Sir, 
that if one were to study the way this Summit had been conducted I am 
referring to the Agra Summit this wo uld be a classic example, which would 
tell us, how not to conduct a summit dialogue. The Prime Minister's 
statement is a bland statement. It does not tell us what our objectives at Agra 
were and what we achieved in that. If we did not achieve what we set out to 
achieve, what were the reasons for it?    Apart from a short 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [8 August, 2001 ] 
statement that the Summit fa iled because of the centrist approach of General 
Musharraf, we don't have a total analys is of what went wrong at the Summit. 
And we have to look at the newspapers to know about the proceedings of the 
National Executive meeting of the Bharat iya Janata Party, to get an idea of 
what exactly happened, because the Pr ime Minister had revealed to that 
National Executive meeting much more than what he has revealed in his 
statement. 
Sir, we have, today, a major problem at our hands'. And I say so, in 
all sincerity, that the failure of the Summit reflects an inadequate preparation; 
but behind this inadequate preparation is the fact that this Government has no 
consistent policy on Pakistan; it has no consistent policy on Jammu and 
Kashmir as well. 
Sir, despite a good deal of white-washing and damage control 
measures that have been undertaken, af ter the results of the Summit became 
known, the sad truth is that the Conference failed; Pakistan walked away with 
the honours, and the whole exercise ended with General Musharraf being 
perceived, both nationally and internationally, in a more advantageous 
position than when he landed in our country. And, I submit to you that first, 
he used the invitation of our Prime Mini ster to crown himself as President. I 
was there in the United States at that time. People were highly critical of 
General Musharraf for having taken this extraordinary step of crowning 
himself as President; but our invitation gave him a degree of legitimacy which 
no other country was willing to provide. Secondly, Sir, he went on a highly 
successful publicity blitz to high light the Kashmir issue and focus 
international attention on it. Thirdly, he managed to hijack the agenda of the 
unstructured summit, pushing our country to the back foot. Fourthly, he won 
the propaganda battle and provided added encouragement to the separatist and 
secessionist elements in Jammu and Kashmir in a manner which was not done 
before. 
Sir, he showed himself as a master of media management, and some 
international analysts whose work I have seen, also came to the coQdusion 
that India was to blame for the failure of the summit. Sir, this reality or these 
perceptions cannot be wished away and I hope that in conducting such 
meetings in the future, we will draw appropriate lessons. 
What about the outcome? We have a Government which is not sure 
even about how to describe the outcome of the summit. The day the summit 
ended, the hon. Foreign Minister made a statement, and I speak 
240 

[8 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
from memory, that there was no br eakthrough, but there was also no 
breakdown, and that the caravan of p eace would move on. That is what he 
said. The next day, we had the spokesman of the Government of India saying, 
"Forget about Agra. If there is to be any future dialogue, we will have to 
begin afresh". Then, again, we have another turnabout and we have the 
statement of the Prime Minister that says, and I quote, "Though we could not 
conclude a joint statement in Agra, we did achieve a degree of understanding. 
We will build on this to further increase the areas of agreement". So, in a 
short period of two weeks, there have been several twists and turnsabout the 
thinking of this Government! 
Sir, before I go further, I hope that the Prime Minister will be kind 
enough to tell us, when he replies to this debate, what is the content of this 
understanding which he has been able to achieve with General Musharraf, 
and on which he hopes that we can build on for a further meaningful 
dialogue. 
Sir, as I analyse what happened at  this summit, I am compelled to 
come to the conclusion that there was no conceptual clarity why this 
Government had invited General Musharraf. There was inadequate 
preparation. There was no clarity about our minimum objectives or even 
adequate awareness of the limitations of  unstructured meetings at the summit 
level. There was no agreed agenda. Th ere was no clear thinking also about 
the intentions and objectives of Pakistan. 
Sir, the Prime Minister and the hon . External Affairs Minister have 
been telling the country that they were surprised by single-minded, focussed 
attention that General Musharraf paid to  the Kashmir issue. I am surprised at 
this naivety. I should be forgiven for using that expression because long 
before General Musharraf came here, he made it quite clear to all and sundry 
that he had a single point agenda and that, whether we agreed with him or not, 
for him Kashmir was the key issue and that progress on all other issues 
depended upon the progress on Jammu and Kashmir, the way he looked at it. 
What is more is, in several press interv iews that he gave to our own leading 
newspapers, he reiterated this position. Further more the delegation that he 
brought with him gave a clear indication that he had no intention of 
discussing any matter other than what he considered to be the core issue, i.e. 
Jammu and Kashmir. Was it not enough for us to draw appropriate lessons 
about the intentions of the adversary we were faced with. For the Government 
now to come up with a statement that the Summit failed because of the single-
minded focus of General Musharraf on 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [8 August, 2001] 
Kashmir, I think, Sir, is a gross under-statement of what happened. It was our 
total failure to anticipate; total failure to devise credible strategies and tactics 
to deal with this expected it was not unexpected, I deliberately say, 'expected' 
onslaught from General Musharraf. It was clearly a case of total lack of 
preparation. 
Sir, this is not the first time and I say so, with great regret, that the 
studied application of mind and long-term thinking, that ought to constitute 
the under-pinning of our foreign policy has been missing in the last two or 
three years. We saw the Pokhran experiment launched with great fanfare --I 
am not going into the merits and demerits of it. We got China trapped into it, 
gave rise to an unnecessary controversy with China; and then the hon. 
External Affairs Minister had to do a lot of explaining, a lot of firefighting, to 
bring the temperature in India-China re lations down. We have seen a similar 
example, very recently, of this mi ssile defence initiative of the U.S. 
Government. We were the first country to rush into embracing this doctrine, 
even when the staunch allies of the United States, like the European Union 
leave aside Russia and China kept a studi ed silence. Later on, I noticed, when 
the hon. External Affairs Minister went to Russia, he tried to modify the 
stand. We tried, later on, to wriggle out of this unambiguous endorsement of 
this. But these are instances where that  studied application, that long-term 
thinking, that long-term under-pinning which is essential for a successful 
foreign policy seem to be missing from the foreign policy experiments of the 
present Government. 
Sir, there was, as I see it, a ba sic confusion about our objectives 
when we went to the Summit. Why do we see it? For two years, this 
Government stated that it would never enter into any negotiations with a 
military dictator, with a military dict ator who was heading a regime which 
was at the root of cross-border terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir. Then, there 
comes a 180 degree turn. Why is this 180 degree turn? It has never been 
explained adequately to Parliament, to public opinion at large, or, to the 
political parties whom the hon. Prime Minister invited from time to time. I 
was present at some of the meetings; reading between the lines, I got the 
impression that this initiative had been taken in order to placate international 
opinion. Beyond that, this Government had no structured design of what is it 
that we wanted to get out of a dialogue with Pakistan. 
Sir, it is, therefore, no t surprising that Pakistan got the feeling that 
India was tired of its involvement in Jammu and Kashmir, and that it could be 
pushed around.  No serious attempt was made to disabuse General

So, Sir, this convinces me that no serious thinking was done before 
we invited General Musharraf, as to what is it that we wanted to get out of 
such a summit. Sir, all over the world,  it is the normal practice, when such 
summits are arranged, that they are preceded by briefings of informal opinion,

the political parties. In one of the meetings with Members of the Congress 
party' we learnt, I think, three-four days before the Summit, that the Summit

our serious doubts about the conduct of a summit without a structured agenda. 
We were assured--! am speaking from memory and I am subject to correction. 
The hon. External Affairs Minister said, "We are still hopeful of a 
breakthrough." 
Sir, it is because of this lack of adequate preparation that a hype was 
allowed to be built up, and we all know how that hype ended; into a deep 
sense of despair. 
Sir, that the media management was poor is something which even 
the Government Spokesmen, including the hon. Prime Minister himself, have 
recognised now. We allowed General Musharraf to use his meetings with 
setect editors, for political gains. We failed to brief our press as skilfully as

Sir, what has this Summit revealed? Both the Prime Minister and the 
External Affairs Minister, in the other House as well as in public, have stated 
that General Musharraf lacked vision and he has no understanding of 
diplomacy. Sir, that may be right. But, you will forgive me, Sir, if I were to

ruthless clarity. He stretched the limits of our endurance by flaunting his 
endorsement of the Hurriyat Conference. And what did we do? With the 
single exception of issuing the invitation to General Musharaff, Indian 
diplomacy showed no trace of being pro-active. It was mostly reactive. Before 
the invitation was issued, General Musharraf was begging to be invited for a 
dialogue at any level at any time, at any place. Any alert and sensitive 
Government would have recognised th at the General was in search of 
legitimacy. We should have, therefore, before extending an invitation to him, 
effectively bargained as to the possibl e outcome of such a conference. I am 
told nothing of that sort was done if I am wrong, I would like to be corrected 
that no serious dialogue took place with the Government of Pakistan before 
inviting General Musharraf. That this thought of inviting him he came to 
know of it, only through the public announcements that were made. 
Sir, it is, therefore, not surprising that several people have 
commented that no serious thinking had been done about our objectives, 
about our strategies for this Summit, that the invitation was born of domestic 
compulsions, notably I hope I am wrong because of the NDA's poor 
performance in State elections and the aftermath of what happened in the 
Tehlaka revelations. In the absence of a structured and coherent thinking, 
India during the Summit was always on the defensive. Musharraf who 
desperately needed this invitation, used it skilfully to turn the tables on us by 
seeking to set the Agenda, redefining the bilateral framework of negotiations 
to make them exclusively Kashmir-centric. 
Sir, General Musharraf's meeting w ith the Hurriyat leaders and his 
public description of Pakistan sponso red terrorists in Jammu and Kashmir as

sufferings  of their families  as  inevitable  in  a freedom  struggle,  his

message that Pakistan's persistence in following the logic of "Two-Nation"

Mr. Jinnah had the vision to realise that for building a prosperous, democratic 
Pakistan, this theory was obnoxious. I quote from what he had said in the 
Constituent Assembly of Pakistan on it* August, 1947. He said, while 
addressing the Members, "You are free to go to your temples. You are free to 
go to your mosques or to any other place of worship in the State of Pakistan. 
You may belong to any religion or caste or creed; that has nothing to do with 
the business of the State. You will find that, in course of time, Hindus would 
cease to be Hindus and Muslims
